verdicts.critic:
Neutrality read of the whole draft, section by section.

TILT. No house verdict anywhere. Basics states shared findings as findings and then lets camps re-read them in their own voice — the National Academies wage result is stated flat in Basics and re-read by Wage Protectionist as confirming the mechanism, which is exactly the right move. The Clemens 50-150% stat carries Borjas's objection and the "stylized modeling exercises, not policy forecasts" caveat in its own detail rather than leaving the number to do rhetorical work. Stat selection skews modestly deflationary of restrictionist alarm (share "risen only modestly," "most have never crossed a border," wage effect ~0, remittances, age-60 fiscal crossover) against three that cut the other way (Gallup 900M, US record foreign-born share, diversity-trust meta-analysis), but every one of those notes carries its counter in the first or second clause, so no reader is misled. One label reads as house-voice framing and is in notes.

PARITY. Twelve positions, all steelmanned in own voice, none strawmanned. Border Sovereigntist (the heaviest camp, weight 44) gets Walzer, Hazony, Murray, CIS, NumbersUSA, Cotton, Reform UK, and — crucially — its non-procedural claim stated plainly ("how many people a country admits in future is a legitimate object of democratic choice"), so it is not reduced to proceduralism, which is the standard way this camp gets flattened. Cohesion Communitarian gets Putnam's mechanism separated from Putnam's policy conclusion, which is the charitable reading. Wage Protectionist gets Borjas's own numbers, the labor-union pedigree, and an honest account of the unsettled Mariel dispute. Depth and citation density are comparable across the field; prevalence weights sum roughly evenly across the restriction and expansion sides and the ordering they produce carries no thumb.

CRUX. The lead ("whose claim the border must answer") is a genuine narrowing, not "both sides have a point," not a binary, not a verdict, and it varies the form away from the question-with-an-or-fork the corpus was over-using. The values block names whose losses count without ruling. But the subtitle does the load-bearing work by enumerating one claimant per camp, and it names ten or eleven for twelve camps: Family Unity Advocate — tier 1, prevalence 19, sixth-heaviest — has no claimant in the list, while camps at weight 8 and 9 do. A family-reunification reader cannot locate their diagnosis in the axis that is supposed to map the field. That is the one blocking defect.

MISSING CAMPS. Judged all three scout candidates. Global Refugee Burden-Sharing is already carried explicitly inside Asylum Rights Defender's detail (the Hathaway/Global Compact wing), so it is not a gap. Faith-Based Hospitality Reformer is the strongest candidate and I came close on it, but its concrete asks distribute across five listed camps and what is distinct is the warrant rather than the diagnosis; its "reject the false binary" positioning is structurally occupied by a twelve-camp field with three middles. Population/Environmental Restrictionist has real proponents but sits below the smallest listed camp in live prevalence, its flagship org is defunct, and the surviving org's current campaigning — which this draft already links, under Wage Protectionist — runs on worker displacement, not carrying capacity. Neither blocks; both are in notes for an editor who wants a thirteenth.

blocking.issue: The crux subtitle enumerates one claimant per camp and omits Family Unity Advocate (tier 1, prevalence_weight 19, sixth-heaviest of twelve) while naming camps at weight 8 (Mobility Partnership Pragmatist, "the worker who wants the job and not the passport") and weight 9 (Origin-Country Advocate, "the country that trained the doctor"; Migrant Labor Rights Defender, "the worker whose legal status belongs to the employer"). The family's claim is not reducible to any listed claimant: "a settled membership" is the existing citizenry, "the long-resident neighbor the law still calls a stranger" is Membership by Presence, "the person in danger" is asylum. A proponent whose whole position is that a spouse or a child is a reason for admission in its own right cannot locate that diagnosis in the axis the crux draws, even though the axis accommodates it perfectly.
blocking.fix: Add the family claimant to the crux subtitle enumeration, in the same register as the others and positioned near the membership claimants: e.g. after "the long-resident neighbor the law still calls a stranger," insert "the spouse or child waiting out a queue on the other side." No other crux field needs changing — the lead, empirical and values blocks are sound.
blocking.quote: crux.subtitle: "Each camp names a different claimant: a self-governing polity, the services that must absorb, a settled membership, an aging economy, the person in danger, the low-wage worker, the worker whose legal status belongs to the employer, the long-resident neighbor the law still calls a stranger, the country that trained the doctor, the worker who wants the job and not the passport, anyone born elsewhere." — no clause corresponds to the Family Unity Advocate position (steelman: "A spouse or a child is a reason of its own, not a category to trade away.").

notes: Basics stat label "Age above which the native-born cost government more than immigrants · US data" headlines the one age threshold at which the fiscal comparison favors immigrants — a framing choice made in house voice. The note underneath is even-handed (it leads with "First-generation immigrants contribute less in taxes than the native-born during their working years") and the detail carries the federal-positive/state-local-negative split, so only the label needs work. A neutral framing of the same finding ("Age at which the per-person net fiscal balance of the native-born and the foreign-born crosses · US data") would carry the fact without the hook.

Crux subtitle: "the services that must absorb" is ambiguous between Cohesion Communitarian (whose claim is about integrating institutions and trust, not services) and Skills Selector ("numbers the economy can absorb"). Sharpening it to name one of them unmistakably would tighten the one-claimant-per-camp mapping.

Question 8 detail is the only question in the set where one side gets the last word inside the other side's paragraph: the "gains erode" paragraph closes with "Expansionists answer that the objection names no threshold: nothing in the literature identifies the scale at which institutional erosion is supposed to begin, and a liberalization taken in steps can be halted at the first sign that it has." Every other question gives each side a clean paragraph ending on its own point. Either drop the rebuttal or give the skeptic a matching reply inside the first paragraph.

Wage Protectionist description ends "the fix is a labor-market lever: slower, more selective inflows, not a wall dressed up in cultural language." This characterizes a neighboring listed camp (Border Sovereigntist) pejoratively from inside another camp's voice, and it is the only such jab in the draft — the other inter-camp boundary statements (Mobility parting from Origin-Country "on direction," Labor Rights against wage protectionism) are substantive rather than dismissive. The camp's self-differentiation survives intact as "not a cultural argument" or similar.

Tier-1 actions run three openness-side (FWD.us, IRC, openborders.info) to one restriction-side (NumbersUSA), with Skills Selector (prevalence 40, second-heaviest camp) below the fold at tier 2 while Open Borders Universalist (prevalence 7) sits above it. Every camp does get an action, and tier/above-fold assignment belongs to the distribution stage rather than this workflow, so this is a flag for that stage rather than a defect here.

Minor pattern worth an editor's eye: the "this is not the extreme version" disclaimer appears in Cohesion Communitarian ("None of this counsels a closed door"), Border Sovereigntist ("not a rejection of immigrants"), Wage Protectionist ("not about who those people are") and Skills Selector ("None of this requires shutting the door"), while Open Borders Universalist, Asylum Rights Defender and Membership by Presence state their maximal claims unhedged. Economic Expansionist, Origin-Country and Family Unity carry the same move, so it is not one-sided, and in each case a real proponent would endorse the disclaimer — but the restriction side carries it more consistently than the expansion side.

Scout candidate judged and rejected — Faith-Based Hospitality Reformer (Evangelical Immigration Table, World Relief, USCCB Justice for Immigrants). Real, currently active, large constituency, and the closest call of the three. Rejected because its concrete program distributes across five listed camps (legalization for the long-resident = Membership by Presence; family reunification = Family Unity Advocate; refugee protection = Asylum Rights Defender; border enforcement = Border Sovereigntist; functioning work visas = Skills Selector), and its distinguishing feature is the theological warrant for claims already on the map rather than a diagnosis no listed camp carries. Its self-positioning as rejecting the open-borders/mass-deportation false choice is also structurally occupied by a field that already contains three middles. If an editor wants a thirteenth position, this is the one to add, and it would need a diagnosis stated in terms no listed camp already carries.

Scout candidate judged and rejected — Population/Environmental Restrictionist (Institute for Sound Public Policy, Kevin Lynn). The carrying-capacity diagnosis is genuinely carried by no listed position, but live prevalence sits below the smallest camp on the board: the flagship org of that tradition is defunct per the scout's own search, the Sierra Club faction lost its fight decades ago, and the surviving org's current campaigning — which this draft already links, under Wage Protectionist, as "petitions on guest-worker visas and the displacement of US workers" — runs on labor displacement rather than ecological limits. Omitting it does not leave a live constituency unable to find itself.

Scout candidate judged and rejected — Global Refugee Burden-Sharing Reformer. Already explicitly carried inside Asylum Rights Defender's detail: "Pragmatists, Hathaway among them, back the Global Compact on Refugees and reformed burden sharing between rich and poor host states, treating orderly resettlement as a necessary supplement to the duty rather than a threat to it." Question 6's limiting reading carries the capacity argument alongside it. No action needed.

verdicts.critic:
Steelman review of the 12-position slice for "Immigration: Open Borders vs. Restriction".

Overall this is a strong positions slice, well above the usual floor: twelve camps, each written in its own idiom, each with a real internal fault line rather than a decorative one, and several places where the draft does the hard thing correctly — Putnam's own liberal reading held separate from what communitarians take from him; Carens split across two camps with the Ethics-of-Immigration argument explicitly insulated from the birthplace-arbitrariness one; Clemens cited for the place premium in Open Borders while the Mobility Partnership section records that he declines the open-borders label; Border Sovereigntist given its substantive half (numbers as a legitimate object of democratic choice) and not left as a procedural argument about enforcement capacity, which is the usual way that camp gets softened. Border abolition (Walia) is present as a distinct thread rather than folded into libertarian open borders, and the Migrant Labor Rights and Origin-Country camps are argued from their own institutions rather than from their opponents' summaries.

Missing-camp scan: no blocking omission. The plausible absentees I tested — climate-displacement recognition, employer/labor-shortage lobbying, ecological-limits restrictionism, deportation abolition — each have their diagnosis already carried by a listed position (Asylum Rights Defender, Economic Expansionist plus Mobility Partnership, Border Sovereigntist, Membership by Presence plus the Walia thread).

One blocking defect, and it is an attribution rather than a framing problem: the Asylum section makes James Hathaway a backer of the Global Compact on Refugees. Hathaway's published position on that instrument is the opposite — his 2018 International Journal of Refugee Law editorial is titled "The Global Cop-Out on Refugees," criticizing the Compact for failing to deliver binding responsibility-sharing. He does champion reformed burden sharing (Hathaway and Neve, 1997), so the fix is small and actually sharpens the camp's internal split rather than blunting it. That is a named proponent made to hold a position he rejects, which is squarely on this dimension.

Everything else is polish: an outsider-sounding clause in the Expansionist wage paragraph, Peri's complementarity claim stranded in the representative note, Borjas's immigration-surplus framing absent from the Wage Protectionist case, an undated Sanders in a proponents list, and an unintroduced "Miller" in the Communitarian detail. None of these would mislead a reader about what a camp believes.

blocking.issue: Asylum Rights Defender, detail paragraph 3: James Hathaway is named as backing the Global Compact on Refugees. This is an authority made to hold a position he publicly rejects — his editorial in the International Journal of Refugee Law (2018) is titled "The Global Cop-Out on Refugees" and argues the Compact failed to deliver the binding responsibility-sharing he has spent his career proposing. As written, the camp's pragmatist wing is anchored to a named thinker who criticized its flagship instrument from within the camp, which weakens both the wing and the split it is meant to describe.
blocking.fix: Cut "Hathaway among them" from the Global Compact clause. Attribute Compact-backing to the actors who actually champion it (UNHCR, the International Rescue Committee, resettlement agencies), and characterize Hathaway by his own position: surrogate protection as the legal theory, plus binding, negotiated responsibility-sharing between rich and poor host states, with the Compact criticized from inside the camp as too weak to deliver it. This makes the intra-camp split sharper — pragmatists who take the Compact as a workable supplement, versus a legal-reform wing that thinks a voluntary compact is the problem — instead of collapsing two wings into one name.
blocking.quote: Asylum Rights Defender / detail: "Pragmatists, Hathaway among them, back the Global Compact on Refugees and reformed burden sharing between rich and poor host states, treating orderly resettlement as a necessary supplement to the duty rather than a threat to it."

notes: Economic Expansionist, detail: "expansionists treat the long-running Card–Borjas dispute as settled in their favor" is an outsider's characterization of motivated reasoning, and it sits asymmetrically against the Wage Protectionist's "The dispute has never fully settled, which this camp reads as reason for caution." One camp is described as prudent about the same literature the other is described as declaring won. In-voice rephrase: the camp holds that the natural-experiment literature, taken together, finds no material aggregate wage damage, and reads the remaining dispute as about a narrow subgroup.

Economic Expansionist: Peri is the representative, but his signature claim — that immigrant inflows raise native productivity and wages through task complementarity — appears only in the representative_note, never in the body. The camp's strongest wage claim is "raises native wages," not "does no material damage"; as written the section argues the weaker of the two.

Wage Protectionist: Borjas's immigration-surplus framing (the aggregate gain is small relative to the redistribution it produces from labor to capital) is the camp's sharpest analytic move and is absent. The section rests on Mariel plus the NAS distributional concentration, which is the empirical case but not the structural one.

Wage Protectionist proponents: Bernie Sanders is listed undated while the detail carefully dates the quote to 2015 and notes the backlash. Dating him in the proponents field (or marking the position as one he argued then) would keep the list from reading as a claim about where he stands now.

Cohesion Communitarian, detail paragraph 3: "Miller defends a democracy's right to cap numbers" is the first mention of Miller in the body, with no introduction, while Goodhart, Alesina and Collier all get one. Give him the same one-clause introduction (David Miller, political philosopher, Strangers in Our Midst).

Open Borders Universalist: keyhole solutions are said to neutralize "the wage, fiscal and cohesion objections," but the institutional-quality objection — the one Collier and Borjas press hardest, and the one Caplan devotes the most space to answering — is not named. Adding it would show the camp meeting its strongest opponent rather than its three easiest.

Asylum Rights Defender: the section is framed entirely in international law. The camp's most-used operative point in the American argument — that anyone physically present may lodge a claim regardless of manner of entry — is absent, which leaves the position looking treaty-bound rather than domestically enforceable.

Mobility Partnership Pragmatist: establishing what Clemens believes by way of openborders.info reads as sourcing a person's position from a neighboring camp's wiki. The substance is right and he has said as much himself; routing it through his own statements would carry it more cleanly and avoid the appearance of letting one camp define another's proponent.

Skills Selector: the evidentiary paragraph rests entirely on the convergence of four national systems. The camp's most-cited quantitative support — the fiscal and earnings gradient by education level — appears only inside other camps' sections, so this one carries its whole evidential load on institutional design rather than outcomes.

prevalence_basis.name: Border Sovereigntist
prevalence_basis.prevalence_basis: The dominant footprint in recent legislation and enforcement budgets across rich democracies, and the platform of several governing or coalition parties.
prevalence_basis.sketch: Deciding who enters is what a self-governing nation is; numbers should fall until the state can enforce its own rules.

prevalence_basis.name: Skills Selector
prevalence_basis.prevalence_basis: The default statutory design in most OECD destination countries — points systems, employer sponsorship, caps; 35% of Americans told Gallup in June 2026 that levels should be kept as they are.
prevalence_basis.sketch: Migration is a policy instrument: admit the numbers and skills the economy and public services can absorb, through legal channels only.

prevalence_basis.name: Cohesion Communitarian
prevalence_basis.prevalence_basis: Holds government in parts of northern Europe and anchors a large political-theory literature on membership and national self-determination.
prevalence_basis.sketch: A generous welfare state and high social trust rest on a settled membership; moderate, well-integrated inflows protect both.

prevalence_basis.name: Economic Expansionist
prevalence_basis.prevalence_basis: Backed by business federations and much of the migration-economics literature; 31% of Americans told Gallup in June 2026 that immigration should be increased.
prevalence_basis.sketch: Aging, shrinking workforces need people; higher legal immigration raises growth, innovation and the tax base.

prevalence_basis.name: Asylum Rights Defender
prevalence_basis.prevalence_basis: Underwritten by binding treaty law and domestic courts and by a large humanitarian and legal-aid sector, though with narrowing legislative support.
prevalence_basis.sketch: Whatever a state decides about economic migration, protection from persecution is a legal obligation, not a quota to be traded.

prevalence_basis.name: Wage Protectionist
prevalence_basis.prevalence_basis: A small but persistent camp: a well-cited labor-economics literature plus a handful of left parties and unions in Europe and the US.
prevalence_basis.sketch: Sustained inflows of competing labor hold down wages at the bottom; restriction is a labor policy, not a cultural one.

prevalence_basis.name: Open Borders Universalist
prevalence_basis.prevalence_basis: Almost no legislative footprint; its standing rests on a well-cited philosophy and development-economics literature.
prevalence_basis.sketch: Birthplace is morally arbitrary; barring peaceful people from where they could work is both unjust and the world’s largest economic waste.
